In Class Five, Hafsa watched her teacher Nirmala's face after every question. When Nirmala's eyebrows rose at "eleven", Hafsa quickly changed it to "twelve", then glanced back to check. She no longer knew which answer she believed. She simply wanted the smile that came when she was right.

At fifteen, Hafsa stood on the wall of the school water tank after a dare, with a ring of classmates cheering and phones raised. Her legs shook. She felt proud and sick at once. Sachin, the sports coach, saw it from the courtyard and walked over fast, staying calm. "Come down slowly, I'm right here," he said, and steadied her hand. Later he sat with her and asked, "What were you proving, and to whom?"

Hafsa was quiet a long while. The next week, when a friend copied her homework, she said no, and it was harder than the wall had ever been. Her voice shook, but it was her own.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa stand after the dare at fifteen?
qa.a: Hafsa stood on the wall of the school water tank.

qa.q: How do Hafsa's behaviour in Class Five and on the tank wall link approval with courage?
qa.a: In Class Five she changes her answers to win the teacher's smile, and on the wall she risks a fall for the cheering crowd, so both come from needing approval; saying no to her friend later serves her own value, which is what real courage does.

qa.q: What was Hafsa probably feeling on the wall, with the crowd cheering and her legs shaking?
qa.a: Hafsa felt proud and frightened at once, wanting the crowd's approval while sick with fear of falling.

qa.q: What did Sachin do that helped Hafsa?
qa.a: Sachin stayed calm, told her to come down slowly, steadied her hand, and later asked what she was proving and to whom.

grounding: Need for approval and the difference between reckless and brave: a child changing answers for a smile and a teenager taking a dangerous dare for an audience.

When the offer from the national institute arrived, Suraj's mother cried and the neighbours brought sweets. Suraj smiled and told himself it was an accident. Somebody had marked the wrong box, or the interview panel was tired. In his first semester he watched classmates solve problems in minutes and felt like a fraud who would soon be found out. He kept quiet in tutorials so nobody could see.

Four years later, at his first job, the feeling had followed him. Suraj arrived before anyone else, stayed until the cleaners came and studied the codebase in his hostel room at night. When he was confused he never asked; asking felt like confessing. His colleague Mahima noticed him rereading the same file for an hour. "Stuck?" she said. He mumbled, "No, just checking."

Weeks later he was still slow, and tired. Mahima sat beside him. "Ask me anything. I asked ten questions a day in my first month." Tenzin, the lead, nodded from across the room.

qa.q: Who noticed Suraj rereading the same file for an hour?
qa.a: His colleague Mahima noticed him rereading the same file for an hour.

qa.q: How are Suraj's thoughts in his first semester and at his first job linked?
qa.a: At the institute Suraj felt like a fraud who would be found out, and at work the same feeling makes him overwork and avoid asking questions, so the imposter feeling shows up as hiding gaps, which slows his learning.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when Mahima asked whether he was stuck?
qa.a: Suraj felt afraid of being exposed, so he denied it and mumbled that he was just checking.

qa.q: What could Suraj try next?
qa.a: He could accept Mahima's offer and ask a question each day, since asking for help exposes less than long hours of hidden struggling.

grounding: Imposter feelings: a student who believes admission to a top college was luck, and the same person overworking and hiding gaps at a new job.

At nine, Jasleen read aloud slowly, stumbling over long words, and her classmates waited. That evening she pushed her book away. "I'm dumb," she said. "I can't read." The next day she stopped raising her hand at all. Her father Ojas sat beside her and asked, "Which words tripped you?" There were only four, and they practised them until bedtime. The label "dumb" shrank to four hard words.

At fifteen, Jasleen was going to interview for a summer job at the library. Her heart hammered, her hands felt cold and she couldn't sit still. "I'm terrified," she told her friend Rafiq. He tilted his head. "You've got the same racing heart as before your trip to the hills. That was excitement." She thought about it, took a breath and said aloud, "I'm excited. I'm nervous, but I'm ready."

Her heart was still racing as she walked into the interview, but now it had a different name.

qa.q: How many words tripped Jasleen when she read aloud at nine?
qa.a: Only four words tripped her.

qa.q: How do the names Jasleen gives herself at nine and at fifteen show the effect of labels?
qa.a: At nine the label "dumb" makes her stop trying, until Ojas turns it into four hard words she can practise; at fifteen she renames a racing heart from terrified to excited and nervous but ready, so the label shapes what she does next.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she told Rafiq she was terrified?
qa.a: Jasleen was anxious and afraid, with her heart hammering and her hands cold, although the same body signals could also mean excitement.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that helped Jasleen at nine?
qa.a: He asked which words tripped her and practised the four hard ones with her, replacing a vague label with a skill that could be practised.

grounding: Labelling: a child's label of dumb that stops effort, and a teenager who names mixed eager and worried feelings as excitement to feel ready.

At five, Kunal pressed himself against his mother Swati's leg at a neighbour's birthday party, his face turned into her skirt. When the host said hello, he shook his head hard. Swati did not push him. She bent, said, "I'll stay right here," and stood beside the cake table until he peeked out. After a long while he took a balloon and let go of her hand.

At nine, a maths worksheet sat on Kunal's desk, full of long division. He looked at it, then suddenly reorganised his bookshelf by colour, sharpened every pencil twice and refilled his water bottle. At eight o'clock the worksheet was still blank and his stomach felt tight. His father Harsha came in, looked at the neat shelves and sat down without a word. "Just the first sum," Harsha said. "I'm here." Kunal took a pencil and wrote the number seven, then eight more lines.

qa.q: What did Kunal take from the party at five?
qa.a: He took a balloon.

qa.q: What do Kunal at five and Kunal at nine show about avoidance, and what worked each time?
qa.a: At five Kunal hides in his mother's skirt and Swati stays beside the cake table; at nine he reorganises his bookshelf and sharpens pencils while the worksheet stays blank, and Harsha sits down beside him. Staying away feels like relief, but the fear remains, and gentle nearness helps him start.

qa.q: What was Kunal probably feeling as he sharpened the pencils twice at nine?
qa.a: Kunal was anxious about the hard division and used easy jobs to escape the fear for a while, though his stomach stayed tight.

qa.q: What did Harsha do that helped Kunal begin?
qa.a: Harsha sat quietly beside him, said he was there, and shrank the task to just the first sum, so Kunal could start.

grounding: Avoidance: a child hiding behind a parent at a party and a schoolboy tidying a bookshelf to escape a hard worksheet, with gentle nearness helping both.

Nine-year-old Kishore slid his maths test under the sofa cushion. It was a 92, and the only mark that mattered to him was the missing eight. His father Yogesh never asked about the game they had played on Sunday or the lunch he had shared. He asked only, "What did you score?" and then, "Why not full marks?" Kishore began to hide any paper with a red cross, and learned to say, "It went well."

His mother Vasudha noticed him rubbing a hole into his notebook while erasing a tiny wrong figure. She felt proud of how hard he tried and worried that he was so afraid of mistakes. That evening she said, "Yesterday I burned the dal and forgot to buy tea. Everybody slips, and ordinary work is enough, you know." She did not tell him to lower his standards. Kishore looked at the notebook and laughed a little, a real laugh for the first time that week.

qa.q: What was the missing mark that mattered to Kishore on his 92 test?
qa.a: The missing eight mattered most to him.

qa.q: How do Yogesh's questions and Vasudha's evening talk show different parental responses to the same child?
qa.a: Yogesh responds only to marks, which makes Kishore feel loved for performance and hide his mistakes, while Vasudha, torn between pride and worry, shares her own mistakes and says everybody slips and ordinary work is enough, without shaming his high standards.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she saw the hole in Kishore's notebook?
qa.a: Vasudha felt proud of his effort and worried about his fear of mistakes, torn between the two.

qa.q: What could Yogesh ask instead of "What did you score?"
qa.a: He could ask about the day, the game and what Kishore enjoyed or learned, so that love does not seem to depend on marks.

grounding: Perfectionism in a household: a child hiding mistakes from a parent who responds only to marks, and another parent worried about tiny errors who shares her own mistakes.

At nine, Gautam brought home a science paper with one wrong answer circled in red. His parents, Pradeep and Sangeeta, studied it and asked, "Why did you lose that mark?" Neither asked what he liked about the experiment. After that, Gautam folded such papers small and hid them in his atlas, and learned to say, "Nothing much."

At twenty-one, Gautam was given a project on water use in his city. He researched for three weeks, redrew the outline eleven times and told his roommate, "It's not ready to show anyone yet." Every version looked flawed to him: the second heading was clumsy, the third source felt weak. Other students were already drafting. Reading one more article seemed safer than writing a single paragraph that could be marked down.

On the deadline's eve Gautam looked at the tidy, untouched document and thought of the atlas. He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence anyway, though his stomach was tight.

qa.q: How many times did Gautam redraw the outline?
qa.a: He redrew the outline eleven times.

qa.q: How is the way Gautam hid papers at nine linked to his endless preparation at twenty-one?
qa.a: At nine Gautam learns that love and approval follow marks, so he hides mistakes; at twenty-one the same fear of a marked-down page keeps him researching and redrawing the outline rather than starting, which is perfectionism as paralysis.

qa.q: What was Gautam probably feeling as he told his roommate the outline was not ready to show anyone?
qa.a: Gautam was afraid of being judged, so preparing felt safer than exposing a rough draft.

qa.q: What small step did Gautam take on the eve of the deadline, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence, which breaks the cycle of preparing because a rough start is easier than a perfect one.

grounding: Perfectionism linked across ages: a child whose parents respond only to marks learns to hide mistakes, and the young adult later postpones starting through endless preparation.
